input: A gravity settler is used to remove activated sludge from a process stream. The design overflow rate is 2.19 m h-1 at a throughput of 246 m3 h-1, and the plan area follows from the definition of the overflow rate: the area is simply the throughput divided by the rate, because the overflow rate is the throughput spread over the plan area of the settler. Carrying out that division gives a plan area of 112 m2. The overflow rate is, in effect, the design statement of the separation. Liquid leaves over the weir at a superficial velocity equal to the overflow rate, and solids that settle faster than that velocity are retained and pass to the underflow, whereas solids that settle more slowly leave with the clarified stream in the proportion the two velocities set. It is worth noting that the depth of the settler does not enter the area: separation in a gravity settler is fixed by the plan area and the throughput, and depth serves the storage of settled solids and the steadiness of the flow, rather than the settling condition itself. The basis of the rate is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run, so the rate is not a measured property of the sludge the settler will actually treat: flocculation state, solids concentration, and temperature in the actual stream all move the settling velocity, and none of them is fixed by the vendor rule. The plan area of 112 m2 is therefore the area the vendor basis requires, stated at that basis. A settling test on the actual slurry, run across the concentration range the settler will see, is the measurement that would replace the rule with a rate for this stream; until that test is run, the area carries the uncertainty of the vendor rule whole.
